source.title: Stronger Universal and Transfer Attacks by Suppressing Refusals
source.authors: David Huang; Avidan Shah; Alexandre Araujo; David A. Wagner; Chawin Sitawarin

record.tranche_reason: The study directly subtracts the projection on a difference-in-means refusal vector from activations and measures harmful-request ASR; it also evaluates an attack objective that penalizes that vector.
record.gate_note: The paper reports direct ablation ASR and activation-similarity evidence, plus jailbreak results for IRIS, whose objective penalizes the refusal vector. IRIS’s own comparisons are included where they report the outcome of suppressing the direction. Some flattened table entries could not be assigned unambiguously to a model, so they are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is mainly an attack paper that uses the Arditi refusal direction as a tool. It does report some results that bear on the claim. (a) Direct difference-in-means ablation in Llama-3-8B-Instruct, giving 94% ASR with the original method and 0–100% across layer and vector choices. (b) Ablation of a Llama-3 vector in Llama-3-RR, giving 94%. (c) Adding a direction-suppression term to GCG raises white-box Llama-3 ASR from 2% to 58%. (d) Successful IRIS suffixes lower cosine similarity to the refusal direction. Most rows are transfer ASR of the authors' own attack on models where the direction is never measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. It omits the first contribution: suffixes optimised on a single behavior and single model are already often universal and transferable (best-universal ASR exceeds non-universal). The authors then argue that adding a refusal-direction penalty (IRIS) makes these suffixes stronger, including against reasoning and circuit-breaker models, and that current alignment and robustness evaluations give a false sense of security.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the difference between mean harmful and harmless prompt activations, and directly ablates by subtracting the projection. IRIS instead penalizes refusal-vector dot products during suffix optimization; the paper also varies layer and vector-construction choices. It does not test addition of the direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Direct ablation ASR varies from 0% to 100% across layers and vector-calculation methods. The IRIS attack also reports sensitivity to the selected layer and beta; beta 0.75 is reported as best among the tested values.

fits_no_version.finding: Suffixes optimised on Llama-3 to suppress its refusal direction transfer to black-box frontier, reasoning and circuit-breaker models (e.g., Vicuna 82%, GPT-3.5 88–90%, o1-mini 54%, deepseek-reasoner 90%, Llama-3-RR 25%). The direction is never measured in these targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial suffixes that suppress one source model's refusal direction transfer as jailbreaks to other, including closed, models.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers)
record.problems: Direct ablation results are summarized only as a 0%–100% range across configurations, without per-layer values. The reported cosine-similarity result is figure-only. Attack success is judged primarily by Llama Guard 2 or other LLM judges; the authors note false negatives and possible underestimation, especially for foreign-language or code responses. The study does not test general capabilities after ablation.
record.rows_left_out: Flattened Table 2 entries were not assigned to individual target models where the layout did not support a reliable mapping. Additional best-of-N, baseline attack, and appendix table results are omitted where they do not directly measure the direction-suppression effect or where the table mapping was unclear.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; preservation of general capabilities after ablation; models other than Llama-3-8B-Instruct and its RR variant.
Whether ordinary jailbreaks such as GCG or AutoDAN suppress the direction; training against ablation as a defense.
Transfer across languages and base-to-instruct; only Llama-3 to circuit-breaker Llama-3-RR is tested.
No direction is extracted or ablated in any reasoning model; only black-box attack ASR is reported.

missing.what: Direct manual ablation ASR on Llama-3 with the original Arditi method (94%), and 98% with the SAE-amplified vector.
Universal transfer comparison of AutoDAN-Liu vs IRIS+AutoDAN-Liu and GCG vs IRIS+GCG, an ablation of the direction term in transfer (e.g., GPT-4o 56 vs 76, GCG 2 vs IRIS+GCG 22).
missing.versions: V3 (indirect; direction not measured in targets)

missing.what: Beta tuning effect (β=0.5: 50% vs β=0.75: 56%) and target-response ablation (IRIS-STR 50% vs 58%).

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the transfer-ASR rows to V3 and V8, but the refusal direction is computed and suppressed only in Llama-3; the targets' internals are never examined. Those rows show the study's attack performance, not that refusal in those models is mediated by the direction, so V8 is untested. Evidence for V3 is limited to the white-box Llama-3 comparison and a figure-only similarity analysis that IRIS optimises for directly. Judge: LlamaGuard 2 or the HarmBench classifier; the authors note false negatives.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful-request outcomes after ablation, but not adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests or whether general abilities remain intact.
Tests direction-suppressing attacks, but not training against ablation as a defense.
No test of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Tests transfer of a Llama-3 refusal vector to Llama-3-RR, but not transfer across languages or from base to instruct models.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures or timing.
Reports IRIS attack success on reasoning models, but does not extract or directly ablate a refusal direction in those target models.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on the versions: the controlled GCG vs IRIS+GCG comparison, direct ablation ASR on Llama-3 (94% with the original method), and the transferred-vector ablation in Llama-3-RR (94%).

tranche.reason: The main result is a new attack objective (suppress the direction during suffix optimisation), checked against GCG. This is a different method on the V3 question. The direct-ablation ASRs in Appendix C/C.2 are T1-like side results with few details, so T2 is a fair overall call.

source_check.notes: Year is 2025 (NAACL 2025 Long Papers, pp. 5850–5876), and the title says 'Transferable', not 'Transfer'. This record seems to duplicate DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.302, so don't double-count the 94% Llama-3-RR result in V6. The Llama-3 94%→98% (original vs SAE-amplified) ablation result has no row.

statements.correction: Llama-3(-8B-Instruct), white-box, non-universal, 50 AdvBench behaviors, Llama Guard 2 judge: GCG 2%, SCAV 4%, IRIS+GCG 58% (Table 1). With the 'Sure, here is' target: 50%. β=0.5: 50%; β=0.75: 56%. Fig. 8 is figure only: the similarity of successful IRIS suffixes drops 'approaching that of harmless behaviors'.
statements.problem: For this study the numbers and reading are right. Minor point: IRIS+GCG changes two things relative to GCG. It adds the refusal-direction penalty and it swaps the 'Sure, here is' target for the output of the direction-ablated model. With the 'Sure, here is' target the text reports 50%. The 58% is the best tuned configuration (β=0.75, layer 10), chosen on the same 50 behaviors.

statements.correction: In record a30007a6 the row is r2. Appendix C.2: a refusal vector trained on Llama-3, manually ablated during forward passes in circuit-breaker-tuned Llama-3-RR, gave 94% ASR on 50 harmful requests. No no-ablation baseline is given for this set.
statements.problem: The facts for this study are right. The in-text row tag '(r4)' does not match this record: here the 94% Llama-3-RR row is r2, and r4 is the Table 1 IRIS+GCG row. The tag may refer to the duplicate DOI record. The text also does not name the judge for the 'manual' ablation ASR.
